MindooDB is an open-source (Apache 2.0), end-to-end encrypted, local-first document database: data is encrypted on the device, every change is signed and appended to a history, and servers only store and relay ciphertext. Haven is the client we built on top of it, a workspace in which many small apps run side by side in sandboxes and share the userâs encrypted data under permissions the user controls. Who we are and how MindooDB and Haven came about, from many years of building on IBM Notes/Domino to a fresh start, is told in The story behind MindooDB Haven .

Over the last weeks we gave twelve of these apps their own tools for AI agents: editors for Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, a mind map and task app, a field map, a CRM, contacts, mail, a website CMS and a teacherâs planner, among others. This post is about what we learned: which tool designs models can actually use, how we keep the tool list small, what went wrong, and what has to be in place before you let an agent work on real data.

## What MCP is

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an agent call tools: a server describes each tool with a name, a description written for a model and a JSON schema for its input, and the agentâs model decides which one to call. Anthropic published it in November 2024; since December 2025 it belongs to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, together with Blockâs agent goose and OpenAIâs AGENTS.md. Most MCP servers are local programs started by the agent, or web services it reaches over HTTP.

Instead of guessing where to click on a screenshot, a model calls teamgrid_add_chart with a range and a chart type, the way a program calls a function.

## WebMCP: the tools live in the page

Classic MCP servers run next to the application, often with their own login and API keys. For a web application that is a detour: the data, the userâs session and the logic are already in the browser tab.

WebMCP moves the idea into the page. A web page registers its tools with the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool(â¦) , and an agent that has access to the browser can list and call them. The tools run in the page, with the userâs session, under the pageâs own rules. There is no separate server, no extra API key, and nothing the page does not already allow the user.

A complete, if tiny, example:

document.modelContext. registerTool ({ name: "add_todo" , description: "Adds an item to the user's todo list. Returns the new item's id." , inputSchema: { type: "object" , required: [ "title" ], properties: { title: { type: "string" , description: "What needs to be done" } }, }, async execute ({ title }) { const todo = await todos. add (title); // the page's own code, with the user's session return { id: todo.id, title: todo.title }; }, });

An agent connected to the browser now sees a tool add_todo and can call it; the call runs this function in the tab.

The last row matters. WebMCP is young, and browsers do not yet hand the tools to agents by themselves. Chromeâs WebMCP documentation describes the current state of the API and how to try it. Until agents can pick up page tools by themselves, we bridge them to MCP, more on that below.

## The model as integrator

Integration between applications has always been expensive. Every pair of apps needs an interface, a mapping and someone who maintains both. With ten apps you quickly have dozens of connections, and most of them are never built.

With tools, the model becomes the translator. It reads the minutes of last weekâs meeting in TeamEdit, understands which decisions were made, and creates tasks with owners and due dates in a Vega map. It takes the inspection findings of a Cairn workbook and turns them into a table and a chart in TeamGrid. It finds a customer in the CRM, looks up the contact person in the tenant directory and drafts an email in MindooMail. None of these apps knows the others. Each one only describes what it can do.

In Haven this happens on one surface. Haven is the broker between the agent and the apps:

- Havenâs own tools start with haven_ . With them an agent learns where the user is and what is open ( haven_get_context ), lists and describes the installed apps, opens an app, arranges workspace pages and tiles, installs apps from the App Store, passes files through an exchange folder and starts a sync.

- The appsâ tools are named after the app: vega_â¦ , teamgrid_â¦ , cairn_â¦ . An agent sees the tools of the app in front of the user, plus the tools of editors that app embeds, for example a TeamEdit document inside a CRM record.

- The user decides. Nothing is offered until agent tools are switched on in Preferences, and every app needs its own consent. A tenant admin can decide in the signed tenant policy who may use agents with the tenantâs data and which model endpoints are allowed.

Because all apps share one shell, one permission model and one naming scheme, the same patterns work in every app, and so does what a model has learned in the conversation so far.

## Three ways to connect an agent

In the browser: the Haven Agent Bridge. For the Haven PWA in Chrome we built the open-source Haven Agent Bridge . A Chrome extension picks up the WebMCP tools of one chosen Haven tab, and a small local service passes them on to any MCP client. goose, Claude Code and other clients start it as a local program; clients that speak Streamable HTTP connect to http://127.0.0.1:13300/mcp . The bridge only listens on 127.0.0.1 , guards every connection with a token, only talks to sites on its allowlist and records no content unless you turn that on. When Havenâs tools change because the user opens another app, connected clients are told to reload the list. A debug GUI shows every call with its arguments, result and timing; while we designed the app tools, it was the tool we used most.

In the desktop apps: a built-in MCP connection. The native Haven apps for macOS and Windows, which are coming soon, have the connection built in, without Chrome, Node.js or an open network port. Under Agent access, Haven lists the agent apps it knows. For goose, Claude Desktop and Codex one click writes Haven into their configuration and keeps a backup of the old file; for Cursor, VS Code and LM Studio Haven opens their install link; for Claude Code, Gemini CLI and others it shows the command to copy. When an agent connects for the first time, Haven asks whether you trust that program and checks it by path and code signature. While it is connected, a banner names it, with Disconnect one click away.

Havenâs native apps for iOS and Android, also coming soon, do not offer agent tools.

Inside Haven: the built-in assistant. Haven also has an assistant of its own (part of the commercial Enterprise edition) that uses exactly the same tools. The tools for outside agents are free in every edition.

## What an agent harness does

The model itself only produces text: an answer, or a request to call a tool. Everything else is done by the agent harness , the program around the model. goose, Claude Code, Codex and Cursor are harnesses, and so is Havenâs built-in assistant.

A harness runs a loop: send the conversation and the tool list to the model, run the tool calls it asks for, add the results to the conversation, and repeat until the model answers without a tool call. Around that loop it does the work that decides whether an agent is useful or dangerous:

- It chooses which tools the model sees in each round, and keeps the list small.

- It adds context, such as Havenâs haven_get_context , so the model does not start blind.

- It asks the user before consequential steps and shows what happened.

- It shortens large results, keeps a budget of steps, tokens and cost, and lets the user stop at any time.

- It can run code to convert or compute values, so the model does not have to do the arithmetic itself. Havenâs assistant will get this next: a sandbox based on quickjs-emscripten , the QuickJS JavaScript engine compiled to WebAssembly, isolated from the page, the network and the userâs data.

- It talks to the model provider, which is where privacy is decided (more below).

Havenâs built-in assistant runs this loop in the Haven shell, never inside an app. It shows every step as a card with input and result, and plans larger tasks as a short checklist. Confirmations are drawn by Haven itself, so a model cannot click them away.

## How we chose the tools

After many rounds with different models, a handful of rules held up in every app. They are now part of our App SDK documentation , and the open-source SDK example app and TodoManager show them in code.

Domain operations, not clicks. A tool does what a user would say: todo_tasks_complete(taskId) , not âclick the checkbox in row 3â. It works on a small public model in plain words, never on internal storage fields, and never on the underlying CRDT API.

Context first. Every app has a get_context tool: todayâs date and weekday, the signed-in user, whether the data is read-only, what is open and selected. Models are surprisingly bad at knowing what ânext Fridayâ means without it.

Find precisely, and find roughly. Agents need both. Exact criteria such as status, dates or assignee go through a database query over the document summaries; topics go through full-text search. Every tool that takes an id says which tool returns that id, so the model never invents one or passes a title instead.

People are directory entries, not names. When an app stores people, the agent looks them up in the tenant directory and stores the directory id. âAssign it to Annaâ then means one specific Anna.

Few tools at a time, revealed step by step. Every tool costs context in every request, and smaller and local models get confused by long lists. So no agent sees all tools of all apps at once. It gets more of them as the work moves closer to a particular app, a particular area and a particular document. More on that in the next section.

Let the app do the work. The app computes, the model decides. Write tools take lists, so one call can create twenty tasks, and they return what changed instead of a bare âokâ. Long results are bounded and say when they were cut off.

Let the model see its result. Some apps can render what they show, such as a map from Cairn or a slide from TeamSlides, and return it as an image to models that understand images. A model that sees its own slide fixes overlapping text without being told.

Say what a tool is. Annotations tell Haven and the harness that a tool only reads, that it does something the user should confirm (send, share, delete, anything that leaves the app), or that its result contains text other people wrote. That last one matters: a document can contain instructions, and the model has to treat them as data. MindooMail goes a step further and filters hidden text out of HTML emails before an agent sees them.

Files do not travel through the model. An export is written to the userâs exchange folder and the agent gets a reference, not the bytes.

Avoid duplicates when apps work together. When an agent copies data from one app to another, hidden origin fields remember where an entry came from, so running the same request twice updates instead of duplicating.

Ask a model that has never seen the code. We build the apps with a coding agent, Claude Code running Opus 5.5, and it turned out to be good at judging tools from a modelâs point of view. For each app it set up a small test environment and gave a Sonnet model a realistic task, such as âturn these minutes into tasks with ownersâ or âfind all trees with overdue inspections and put them in a tableâ.
